newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian cenbank sees no change in forex policy.
newsitem.headline: Colombian cenbank sees no change in forex policy.

text.p: Colombia's central bank is not planning any immediate changes in monetary policy to help stop the Colombian peso's recent rise against the dollar, a bank official said.

Salomon Kalmanovitz, one of seven members of the bank's board of directors, said the bank's daily floating rate exchange band was likely to be altered next year, but he ruled out any swift devaluation or an elimination of the exchange rate band.
"It's the only thing that has worked well for us," Kalmanovitz said of the exchange rate band.

The peso has gained about 5.7 percent since early June, when it was trading at 1,074 to the dollar, prompting repeated demands from the government and exporters for a devaluation to help make Colombian goods more competitive in the global marketplace.

But Kalmanovitz, who spoke in a telephone interview with Reuters, said the central bank had no plans to undercut it artificially as long as it stays within its daily trading band, which was set Wednesday at 976.76 to 1,123.80.

The peso has lost just 3.0 percent of its value against the dollar so far this year, and Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said Wednesday he hoped the bank would adopt measures to ensure that it falls an addede 10.5 percent by year-end in line with government targets set at the start of 1996.
Kalmanovitz said no formal proposal in that sense had been forthcoming from Ocampo, however.

In the interview, he said a series of factors had lifted the peso from where its was earlier this year, when the bank was forced to sell $400 million in reserves to lift the local currency off the bottom of local trading floors.

Positive factors for the peso include an easing of the country's political crisis and rising foreign investment. But Kalmanovitz said the state oil company, Ecopetrol, was also putting upward pressure on the peso by bringing more dollars back into the country than it needs to cover its operating costs. The excess greenbacks are being handed over to government to help cover its own operating costs, he said.

Kalmanovitz, who said he expects to see the peso trading between 1,020 and 1,030 to the dollar by year-end, said the central bank expects the government's fiscal deficit to rise to 1.8 percent of gross domestic product this year.

Because of the deficit, Kalmanovitz said the central bank was likely to change the peso's exchange band next year, when it expects it will buy $1 billion to help absorb the excess amount of dollars flowing into the country. "The impact of the external financing of the deficit is going to be bad," he said.
